claims.text: Greg LaVecchia argues that the foundational self-development question for a 17-year-old is: which of my beliefs do I hold because others told me to hold them, versus which did I choose independently? Specifically: do I pursue a college path because parents demanded it, eat a certain way because they dictated it, or chase a career because society prescribed it? Without asking this, a person is executing others' programming rather than developing genuine agency.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: early stage of life, roughly age 17
person has not yet consciously examined inherited beliefs
claims.mechanism: External programming from family and social environment accumulates as implicit beliefs that drive behavior; without examination these operate as invisible constraints, preventing the development of self-directed identity.
bounded_by: Does not address adults who have already engaged in this examination

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia asserts that frustration experienced at age 17 is often a product of low free agency: being told what to do without having developed the capacity to think independently creates inner conflict even when the person cannot yet name the source of that frustration.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: person is being directed by parents or authority figures
claims.mechanism: Frustration arises when action is dictated externally but the person lacks the framing to recognize that low agency is the cause; the absence of self-directed thought blocks both the feeling of freedom and the ability to diagnose why.

examples.text: Greg LaVecchia uses three concrete domains to illustrate inherited versus chosen beliefs at age 17: attending college because parents insisted on it, eating in a specific way because it was the family norm, and pursuing a prescribed career path. In each case, the person was executing an external directive without evaluating whether it matched their own judgment. LaVecchia notes that he experienced this at 17 himself — lots of frustration, being told what to do, but not yet thinking for himself.

practices.text: At age 17, audit every major belief and life direction you currently hold and ask: did I arrive at this independently, or did someone tell me to have it? Begin distinguishing inherited programming from genuine self-direction as the first step toward developing free agency.
If you are asking questions about how to think for yourself at a young age, treat that as evidence you are ready to begin — the question itself signals sufficient self-awareness to handle the answer.
